title: What's my line?
author: Eaton, Lance
summary: Drawing from a workshop on AI in scholarly writing and research, Lance Eaton argues that clear guidance on AI use in academia comes down not to universal rules but to each scholar identifying their personal 'line'—what they do, why, and what they value as a researcher. Workshop participants (independent scholars, faculty, students) showed a revealing pattern: 310 responses across five workflow stages skewed toward AI refining, editing, and adversarial stress-testing of the scholar's own thinking rather than AI originating the thinking itself. The unspoken principle that emerged: AI may interrogate or compress content the author has already engaged with, but should not be the workhorse of thinking itself. Eaton gives practical guidance on treating AI use as a methodology (document it, disclose it, track chatlogs), thinking about version-history tools as a paper trail, and building a community of practice to navigate a technology that will be in flux for at least a decade. The essay closes with a self-reflective exercise: map your scholarly identity, your purpose, what you are comfortable exporting to AI, and what you hold onto.
points: The 'it depends' answer is not a hedge but an honest description of where AI scholarship is. What it depends on most is who you are as a scholar, what drives you, and what you value. Before following anyone else's guidelines, the work is to answer those questions for yourself.

Treat AI use as a methodology. Document what you used, for what purpose, at what stage, and with what results. Including chatlogs or links to AI sessions at the bottom of a document is a concrete starting practice that makes the process auditable and honest.

The skills we develop through scholarly work are like muscles: if we don't use them, we lose them. AI can help us surface our thinking and challenge our arguments, but if it replaces the cognitively demanding work of forming ideas, the skill atrophies—including the ability to defend the work we put our names on.

We are in a transitional middle space that the internet analogy suggests could last 15 to 20 years before norms stabilize. In that instability, transparency is the most defensible posture: if your AI use is visible, mistakes become learning conversations rather than integrity violations.
quotes: The question I keep coming back to when folks are looking for clearer guidance is: what's my line? We should all be answering this. Maybe some of us can come up with a global answer. I suspect more of us will need to just think about it contextually.

If this chatlog was shared in tandem with my work, would people determine that my work wasn't sufficient enough to claim as 'mine'? You may not have perfect answers for that. But you need to have that conversation with yourself.

Can you authentically stand behind everything in that piece that was created? Can you justify every piece of knowledge, insight, and angle? Because if you're putting something forward with your name on it, that's what you have to do. Authorship means 'this fully represents me.'

Many of our skills are like our muscles: if we don't use it, we lose it. Recognizing the skills impact, it means we should raise our reflective attention to our usage. Ask yourself with each use: Why am I using this? What's leading me to use this?

At the end of the day, all of this boils down to: what kind of scholar, researcher, educator, scientist, writer do you want to be? None of the different tips, tactics, and guidance that is out there matter unless you can answer this question and hold yourself to that.
